clinical_knowledge.topic: Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with IV albumin replacement if large volume, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: swollen abdomen and yellowing of the eyes over the past month

Key HPI features: 4-week progressive abdominal distension with ankle swelling and mild scleral icterus. Reports early satiety due to abdominal tightness, dark tea-coloured urine, and easy bruising. Denies haematemesis, melaena, or acute confusion, though spouse notes mild sleep disturbances.

Objective/Exam findings: Check vitals, weight, abdominal girth. Examine for stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, caput medusae, shifting dullness, asterixis). Bloods: LFTs, INR/PT, albumin, FBC, U&Es. Diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, cell count to rule out SBP).
Relevant background/PMH: alcohol use disorder (heavy drinking 80g/day for 25 years, abstinent for past 4 months), hypertension
Current medications: thiamine 100mg OD, spironolactone 100mg OD (started recently by GP)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Confusion or drowsiness — suggests hepatic encephalopathy.
management_principles: Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with IV albumin replacement if large volume
Initiate lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 57M with history of alcohol dependence presents with progressive ascites, peripheral oedema, jaundice, and sleep reversal over 4 weeks. No GI bleeding reported.
reference_soap.objective: Check vitals, weight, abdominal girth. Examine for stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, caput medusae, shifting dullness, asterixis). Bloods: LFTs, INR/PT, albumin, FBC, U&Es. Diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, cell count to rule out SBP).
reference_soap.assessment: Decompensated alcohol-related liver cirrhosis with ascites and mild hepatic encephalopathy. DDx: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression, portal vein thrombosis.
reference_soap.plan: Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with IV albumin replacement if large volume. Optimize diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide ratio). Initiate lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis. Ultrasound abdomen with Doppler and alpha-fetoprotein to screen for HCC. Hepatology referral.

learning_objectives: Elicit a detailed alcohol history quantified in units/grams and assess duration of abstinence
Screen systematically for complications of cirrhosis: ascites, variceal bleed risk, hepatic encephalopathy, SBP
Explain the rationale behind sodium restriction, diuretic therapy, and paracentesis
Provide compassionate communication surrounding liver disease prognosis and relapse prevention

teaching.diagnosis: Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites
teaching.one_liner: Years of heavy drinking have scarred the liver; it can no longer make enough protein or clear fluid, so fluid pools in the abdomen and legs and the skin turns yellow.
red_flags: Confusion or drowsiness — suggests hepatic encephalopathy

must_ask.say: When did your belly start to swell, and has it been getting bigger?
How much alcohol were you drinking, and when did you last have a drink?
Has anyone noticed you seeming confused, forgetful, or sleeping differently?
Have you noticed your skin or eyes turning yellow, or your urine getting darker?
Have you noticed bruising more easily than before?
Does the swelling make it hard to breathe or lie flat?
Are you taking your water tablets exactly as prescribed?

history.answer: My stomach has been swelling up like a balloon and my eyes look yellow over the last month.
Mainly my belly is swollen huge, and both of my ankles and lower legs are swollen as well. My face and hands are not puffy.
It started gradually about four weeks ago and has been getting steadily worse each week.
The swelling in my legs gets a bit worse toward the evening, but my belly stays tight and bloated all day and night.
Yes, when I take my socks off in the evening, they leave deep indentations that take a while to fade.
I've gained around ten pounds over the past month, even though I haven't been eating nearly as much as usual.
No, neither leg is red, hot, or painful. Both legs are swollen equally.
I get winded when walking up stairs or bending over because my swollen belly pushes up against my chest.
I can't lie completely flat because my stomach feels too tight and suffocating, so I sleep on three pillows. I haven't woken up gasping for air in the middle of the night, though.
My urine has turned dark brown like strong tea, and I think I'm passing a bit less of it than usual. There's no foam or blood in it.
My belly feels stretched tight to bursting. I get full after just a few bites of food because there's no room left in my stomach.
Yes, I've noticed large purple bruises popping up on my arms and legs even when I haven't bumped into anything. My gums also bleed a bit when brushing.
No, I have never vomited blood or coffee-ground material, and my bowel movements are normal brown, never black or sticky.
I don't think I've been confused, but my wife says I've been mixing up day and night, staying awake all night and napping during the day.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
It doesn't hurt sharply, but it feels constantly heavy, tight, and stretched.
No, I haven't had any sore throat, cough, skin infection, or recent illness.
I feel tired and worn down, but I haven't had unusual sensitivity to the cold, constipation, or dry skin.
My bowels move once a day normally, with no diarrhea. My appetite is poor because my stomach feels crammed.
No, I haven't had any surgeries, long flights, periods of bed rest, cancer, or hormone treatments.
I do not take any anti-inflammatory painkillers, steroids, or blood pressure drugs like amlodipine.
I've been trying to cut down on salt since my doctor told me to, and I spend most of my day resting at home because moving around is tiring.
I think my liver is finally struggling and giving up from all the heavy drinking I did in my past.
I'm terrified that my liver has completely failed and that I only have weeks left to live.
I was really hoping you could drain this fluid from my stomach today so I can breathe and sleep comfortably again.
Yes, I take the water pill and the vitamin every single morning without missing any doses.
I've had high blood pressure for five years, and I had alcohol addiction for many years. No diabetes, kidney disease, or heart conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital overnight.
My GP recently started me on spironolactone one hundred milligrams daily and thiamine one hundred milligrams daily.
I don't have any allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
I smoke about ten cigarettes a day and have smoked for around thirty years.
I used to drink heavily for twenty-five years, around eighty grams of alcohol every day, but I quit completely four months ago and haven't touched a drop since.
I am currently unemployed and live at home with my wife, who takes wonderful care of me.
My father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of liver disease, kidney failure, or heart problems.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.8°C; body weight increased by 5 kg.
Mild scleral icterus present bilaterally; conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Multiple spider nevi on the upper chest and shoulders, with mild palmar erythema on both hands; no skin excoriations.
Jugular venous pressure is normal at 2 cm above the sternal angle; no jugular venous distension noted.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no S3 gallop, S4, or cardiac murmurs.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without crackles or wheezes; mild reduction in lung expansion at the bases.
Distended, protuberant abdomen with an everted umbilicus and visible superficial venous collaterals; no hernia seen.
Abdomen is tense but non-rigid; mild generalized discomfort on deep palpation, without focal tenderness, guarding, or rebound tenderness.
Positive shifting dullness and fluid wave, consistent with moderate-to-large ascites.
Bilateral symmetric 2+ pitting edema extending from feet up to mid-shins.
Calves are symmetrical without tenderness, warmth, erythema, or cord-like induration.
Subtle asterixis demonstrated on sustained dorsiflexion of the wrists; no resting tremor.
